## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all visible wavelengths, and when it enters the atmosphere it collides with the tiny gas molecules (primarily nitrogen and oxygen). These molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of light, so they scatter the light in a wavelength-dependent way: shorter wavelengths (blue and violet) are scattered far more strongly than longer wavelengths (red and orange). This scattered blue light is redirected in all directions and reaches our eyes from across the sky, giving it its characteristic blue color. (A common follow-up is why the sky isn't violet, since violet has an even shorter wavelength—the answer is that the Sun emits less violet light, some of it is absorbed higher in the atmosphere, and our eyes are simply more sensitive to blue than to violet.)

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the **fourth power of the wavelength**:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This strong dependence explains why blue light (~450 nm) scatters roughly **5–6 times more** than red light (~650 nm), which is the physical basis for the blue sky—and also why sunsets appear red, as the longer path through the atmosphere at sunset removes most of the scattered blue, leaving the transmitted red light.
